content_summary: WHAT IT IS: Exploratory evaluative case study of the Giulio34 CLT, 34 Corso Giulio Cesare, Aurora district, Turin, described as one of the first Italian CLTs and 'the first property in Italy purchased through a CLT'. Promoter: Porta Palazzo Community Foundation (established 2020, grassroots housing group, with design team Follow The Architect). Land holder: a dedicated foundation, 'Community Land Trust - Terreno Comune ETS Foundation', set up spring 2024 as trustee and fiduciary manager of the land (a foundation chosen over an association or cooperative because it can hold land fiduciarily and structure participatory governance). Acquisition: deed signed 1 July 2024; total initial investment EUR 516,450 = EUR 445,000 purchase + EUR 71,450 ancillary/technical/legal; funded by solidarity loans from 82 individuals and 5 local organisations raising about EUR 500,000. Renovation: about 74% of project costs; funded by grants, bank loans and social loans, plus sale of some units to partner third-sector organisations. EUR 28,000 from the municipal 'ImpatTO' call (selected March 2025) for community spaces; two of three ground-floor units reconverted to neighbourhood use. LEGAL DEVICE: Italian 'surface right' (diritto di superficie) stands in for the Anglo-Saxon ground lease: buyers acquire the dwelling via a surface right, the Foundation keeps the land and common spaces. Duration of the surface right is still under evaluation: 30 years or more, renewable if constraints are respected (note: not the 99-year lease of the classic US model). RESALE TERMS (designed, preliminary, not yet final): appraisal-based 'improvements-only' formula per the CLT Technical Manual (White 2011): resale price = original price plus a limited share, up to a maximum of 25% of the increase in value, covering maintenance and inflation compensation; land value excluded from the calculation; resale only to the Foundation or to households on its waiting list; owner-occupation required, letting prohibited except Foundation-authorised cases or units held by third-sector organisations; no sale on the open market. Governance: tripartite board (one third residents, one third members sharing the project's values, one third general interest including public bodies/universities/housing networks) activates only after units are sold; until then a provisional steering board and open consultative body. Targets households 'in the grey zone' excluded from both private market and public housing; total monthly housing cost (mortgage, surface-right fee, condominium, utilities) targeted around one third of income. METHOD: three dimensions: access value (CLT price vs comparable full-ownership market price, in EUR/m2 and %), retention value (presence and design of resale/transfer controls, not measured outcomes), social value (proxies: community finance converted to a collective asset, reuse of a degraded building, ground-floor neighbourhood spaces, third-sector involvement, planned tripartite governance). Data April 2024-January 2026: three interviews, document analysis, fieldwork and meetings; market check in January 2026 by 'comparative single-parameter estimation' from listings (Immobiliare.it, Idealista, Casa.it), comparables matched on typology, surface, state of renovation, balconies, construction period and floor. QUANTIFIED RESULTS: (1) The CLT applies a 'surface rights value coefficient of 75%', i.e. subtracts an assumed 25% land component; so CLT sale prices are 'approximately 25% lower than the estimated market values for comparable units in the local market of the whole city of Turin' (the Foundation's estimate); abstract: 'approximately 25% below comparable full-ownership values'. (2) Aurora market benchmarks, January 2026: about EUR 1,680/m2 (two-room), 1,830/m2 (three-room), 1,940/m2 (four-room); the paper says the reduction 'remains significant' against these but the CLT price per m2 sits only in the unextractable Figure 6. (3) Aurora context: OMI (Italian Revenue Agency) H2 2025 values EUR 1,300-1,900/m2 for economic-type dwellings; 21% of building stock severely degraded vs about 11% city average; density 18,580 inhabitants/km2 vs 6,710; 29.5% of residents rent; 1,354 court-ordered evictions in 2024 (just under four a day). LIMITS (the paper's own): retention not observed (no resale yet; 'cannot yet establish the effectiveness of the mechanism in definitive terms'); final contracts, resale rules and household selection are preliminary; the 25% gap 'should not be attributed mechanically to the legal separation of land and buildings alone' because philanthropic/community finance enabled acquisition, the acquisition price is low because the building is degraded, and 74% of costs go to renovation; financial sustainability not secured (grant delays, cost overruns, bank-debt repayment); legal architecture untested in Italy (fee's legal nature, bankability, enforceability of resale restrictions); governance in transition, risk of dependence on a few promoters; context-dependent, 'not an automatically replicable solution'. GEORGIST HOOK for the page: the paper reads the CLT as removing land value (ground rent capitalised into price) from the transaction and retaining part of publicly produced land value collectively; it cites Davis (CLT Reader), DeFilippis, Lowe and Pierce, not Henry George; the land share is an administrative coefficient (25%), not an estimated site value. Do not describe it as a land-value measurement.
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/community-land-trust.md (last_reviewed 2026-07-07) covers the classic US model (99-year ground lease, resale formula, tripartite board), origins (New Communities Inc. 1969; Borsodi/Swann; 1972 Guide), Howard precedent, Relation to Georgism, scale (Champlain Housing Trust), Rosenberg 2026 (Lincoln, conservation trusts) and Lithgow & Wall 2026 on ACME (abstract unavailable). It has no European case, no Italy/Turin content, and no quantified affordability evidence; it acknowledges the resale formula limits owner wealth-building. No research/ page on CLT affordability exists (grep of research/ shows barnes-sky-trust, branzoli-caiumi-italy-ace only). Corpus digest has no Turin/Giulio34 page. Related pages for inbound links: concepts/land-value-capture, concepts/land-as-commons, concepts/community-land-trust.
uncertainties: 1) THREE FACTS FOR T1 TO CHECK: (a) the ~25% discount is the Foundation's own estimate against a Turin-wide market benchmark and is partly built in by the 75% coefficient (a stated assumption), so it is not an independent measurement of land value; (b) Figure 6 (CLT EUR/m2 prices) is an image, so T1 should open the MDPI page to read the actual per-flat prices and the Aurora comparison rather than rely on the prose; (c) retention/resale terms (25% cap on appreciation, surface right of 30+ years) are 'under evaluation' from preliminary documents, so state them as the project's current design, and do not give them as the legal terms. 2) Affiliation discrepancy: Todella is at Parma (Crossref), not Politecnico di Torino; verify on the MDPI page. 3) The paper's introduction frames the problem as land-value capitalisation into prices (Georgist adjacent) but it does not cite George, Gaffney or the LVT literature; avoid saying it 'tests' Georgism. 4) 'Quoted material' rule: any quote needs a locator; the text has no page numbers (HTML), so cite section numbers (4.2, 4.3, 5). 5) Reference list was not read except the Crossref entries for refs 2, 3, 5, 7, 12, 14, 16, 17, 37; the claims about the wider CLT literature were not checked against those sources. 6) Not read: MDPI peer-review history/dates, funding statement and conflict-of-interest statement (not in the extracted text).

verdict: ENRICH, narrowly: (1) concepts/tax-capitalization.md: one short 'Current debate' paragraph (Tier 2 think-tank commentary, status stated) saying that commentators at the Independent Institute argue that 2026 homeowner property-tax cuts will be capitalised into higher prices rather than lower housing costs, with the empirical basis for that mechanism pointed to the wiki's Tier 1 pages (Oates 1969, Palmon & Smith 1998, Hoj-Jorgensen-Schou 2017, Coven et al 2026), and with the caveat that capitalization is complete for land but depends on supply elasticity for improved housing. (2) places/wyoming.md: one sentence in 'The November 2026 Ballot Measure' placing Initiative 1 among the 13 statewide property-tax measures in seven states counted by Ballotpedia (12 remain for 3 November after Louisiana Amendment 4 was defeated on 16 May), cited to Ballotpedia plus the Wyoming SoS source already there. NO NEW page now: the article itself is thin, the 13-measure list is an aggregator's, and a 2026 ballot-measure event page should wait for the 3 November results (T1's call; if wanted, build it from the states' own legislative texts, not from this article). DO NOT use the article's own state list (see uncertainties). Not a REJECT because the Ballotpedia cross-check is useful to the wiki and the capitalization mechanism is on-topic.
claim_grade: D for the article as a source of fact or evidence (opinion commentary by a think tank, no studies cited for the capitalization claim; its one link for it is a Florida business-magazine piece; it contains at least one demonstrable error on the state list). The capitalization claim itself is a standard B/C-level theoretical point already supported on the wiki by Tier 1 sources, so the wiki does not need this article for it. Source tier (§4c): the Independent Institute is a think tank, so its commentary is Tier 2: origin/proponent only, with status stated, never in a lead and never as support. Authors by rubric: Shelton Weeks is Lucas Professor of Real Estate and Director of the Lucas Institute for Real Estate Development & Finance at Florida Gulf Coast University (a founding faculty member), per the article's own bio; he is a real-estate/finance professor, not an economics professor as the task note says. Nikolai Wenzel is a research fellow of the Independent Institute and of the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER) and 'Professor of Economics at Universidad de las Hespérides', where he directs the MA and PhD in economics, per the article's bio; Universidad de las Hespérides could not be verified here, so Wenzel's academic standing on this topic is unverified and his two think-tank fellowships are advocacy-body affiliations. Neither is on the people-tiers list; by the rubric treat both as Tier 2 for this commentary (credentialed, but the piece is advocacy and the authors state a prior: 'we favor tax cuts'). Ballotpedia (the source for the measure list) is a secondary aggregator: B for the roster and measure descriptions, which it sources to state legislatures and ballot titles.
content_summary: THE ARTICLE (no study or dataset is analysed): Authors say the U.S. has had 31% inflation since December 2019 and the Case-Shiller national index is up 55% in that time; blame monetary policy and zoning/regulatory supply limits; note Congress's 'ROAD to Housing Act' (caps institutional ownership at 350 single-family homes). Then: 'In the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections, seven states are featuring a total of 13 constitutional measures aimed at lowering housing costs through property tax reductions' (links Ballotpedia); 'almost double the historical average' of property-tax discontent per cycle over 50 years (no source). CAPITALIZATION ARGUMENT (one paragraph): 'Lower property taxes are unlikely to reduce housing prices. If anything, they will likely put further upward pressure on prices... tax savings will likely be capitalized into property prices. Indeed, a would-be property buyer considers the entire cost of housing... Lower property taxes mean more money is available for housing; in turn, the resulting increase in demand will lead to higher home prices.' Evidence cited for it: none beyond a link to a Gulfshore Business (Florida) article. REST OF THE ARGUMENT: local governments must cut services or raise other taxes or move to state funding (loses local autonomy, grows state bureaucracy), cites Arthur Seldon and Buchanan & Tullock only as general references; compares the seven states on sales-tax rank, income-tax rank, Economic Freedom of North America 2025 (Fraser Institute) rank and debt-to-GDP (Florida lowest, under 1%; Louisiana 4.8%); notes the federal debt (0.1tn, about 125% of GDP). RECOMMENDATION: no concrete policy recommendation; 'we are instinctively in favor of lower taxes' but 'supporters of property tax reform should ask themselves if the downside risk is worthwhile', and states should plan for alternative revenue first. THE 13 MEASURES, per BALLOTPEDIA (not per the article, which names states only): Florida (2): Amendment 3 (homestead exemption for non-school taxes raised from $25,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028; non-homestead assessment cap cut from 10% to 5%; limits on use of local property tax revenue; legislative staff estimate local revenue loss of $4.6bn in FY2027-28 and $8.4bn in FY2028-29; placed by HJR 1 in the 1-3 June 2026 special session, House 75-26, Senate 30-9) and an Agricultural Property Exemption Amendment (Ballotpedia's campaign table calls it Amendment 2; tangible personal property used for agriculture/agritourism). Georgia (1): Agriculture and Timber Amendment (acre cap for conservation-use valuation from 2,000 to 4,000 acres). Louisiana (5 total, one already decided): Amendment 4 of 16 May (business inventory exemption; DEFEATED); on 3 Nov: Surviving Spouse Amendment (disabled-veteran homestead exemption transfer), Senior Exemption Amendment (new exemption for 65+, $6,000 to $30,000 of assessed value), Property Tax Rate Limits Amendment (rates after reassessment up to existing voter-approved maximums), Special Assessment Amendment (income limit for assessment freeze raised from $100,000 to $150,000), Rehabilitated Property Amendment (optional exemption for blighted property). North Carolina (1): Property Tax Levy Limit Amendment (legislature to limit local levy increases). Oklahoma (1): State Question 847 (assessment growth limit 5% to 4% generally; homesteads/agricultural 3% to 1.75%; senior freeze rules revised). Tennessee (1): Amendment 2 (bars the General Assembly from imposing a state property tax; Tennessee has none today; local taxes unaffected). Wyoming (1): Initiative 1, a citizen-initiated STATUTE (not a constitutional amendment) for a 50% exemption of assessed value of a primary residence. Ballotpedia's breakdown: 4 homeowner exemptions, 3 assessments, 4 agriculture/business/non-residential, 1 rate authority, 1 prohibition on imposing property taxes. All 12 remaining are on the 3 November 2026 ballot. Ballotpedia: voters decided 58 statewide property-tax measures in 2020-2025, approved 45 (77.6%), defeated 13. TIER 1 STUDIES THE ARTICLE CITES: none. The wiki's Tier 1 capitalization sources (already on tax-capitalization.md and proposition-13.md) are Oates 1969 (JPE), Palmon & Smith 1998 (JPE), Hoj-Jorgensen-Schou 2017 (Danish Economic Councils), Ferreira 2010 (J Public Econ, Prop 13 benefits), O'Sullivan-Sexton-Sheffrin 1995/1999 and Coven-Golder-Gupta-Ndiaye 2026 (NBER 35587).

No wiki page for Florida Amendment 3, Tennessee Amendment 2, Oklahoma SQ 847, the Louisiana, Georgia or North Carolina measures; no 2026-ballot-measure overview page; the related page is events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md (opposite direction, LVT enablement).
uncertainties: THREE FACTS FOR T1 TO CHECK: (1) The task note says '13 November 2026'; the election day is 3 November 2026 (Ballotpedia: 'The remaining 12 measures will appear on the November 3 ballot') and the article says only 'November 2026 midterm elections'; 13 is the number of measures, not a date. Also, of the 13, one (Louisiana Amendment 4) was defeated on 16 May, so 12 are on 3 November. (2) The article's state list contradicts Ballotpedia: the article names Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Wyoming and builds its sales-tax, income-tax and debt comparisons on those seven; Ballotpedia lists Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Wyoming (no Indiana or Kansas measure appears anywhere on its page). The authors link Ballotpedia as their source, so the discrepancy is theirs (or Ballotpedia's roster changed); confirm against the states' own legislative texts before naming any state as 'on the ballot'. Also the article calls them 'constitutional measures' and 'tax cuts to lower housing costs'; Wyoming's is a statute, and several measures are agriculture/business exemptions, rate-authority or assessment limits, with one that may RAISE some local flexibility (Louisiana rate-limits) and one that bans a tax Tennessee does not levy; only about four are homestead-exemption measures. (3) Author standing: Weeks is a real-estate professor (not an economist) and Wenzel's university could not be verified; treat the piece as Tier 2 commentary. OTHER: the capitalization paragraph is the standard demand-side argument; it is complete only for land, and for improved housing the incidence depends on supply elasticity (the article itself says supply restrictions are the root problem), so the wiki should not state 'tax cuts raise home prices' as a general finding; no Tier 1 study of the 2026 measures exists yet. Official state sources found through Ballotpedia but not opened: Florida HJR 1 (2026 special session, passed 2 June 2026), Tennessee HJR 81 (2023-24) and SJR 1 (2025-26), Oklahoma SJR 39 (2026), plus the Wyoming SoS ballot document the wiki already cites. The article's macro claims (31% inflation, 55% Case-Shiller, Fed monetising $4tn, debt $40.1tn) were not checked and should not be used.

content_summary: WHAT THE PAGE SAYS (the organisation's own account): In 1943 the Canadian land economist H. Bronson Cowan, 'director of the International Research Institute on Real Estate Taxation', visited Melbourne to conduct research in the municipalities of Brunswick and Camberwell; 'his techniques inspired a number of local professionals to form the Land Values Research Group (LVRG)'. The page does not give an explicit founding year or date for the LVRG itself, only the 1943 visit as the inspiration (the wiki's Kavanagh page gives 'founded in 1943' from the 2011 press release; see uncertainties). FOUNDING DIRECTOR: Allan R. Hutchinson BSc MIEAust (1907-1988); under him the LVRG published '37 major documents', including (per the page) world-leading empirical studies that site-value rating is more conducive to growth than systems taxing buildings; 'Hutchinson's contribution was to quantify the damage done by taxing buildings'. SUCCESSION: on Hutchinson's death in 1988 he was succeeded by Bryan Kavanagh, a professional property valuer; Kavanagh predicted in The Valuer (July 1987) that the next recession would be 1991/2 ('correct to within one year'); aggregating state property-turnover statistics since 1972 he found that whenever turnover exceeded 19% of GDP in a nationwide trend and then fell back below 19%, recession followed within two years; he concluded the ratio of property turnover to GDP is 'a veritable barometer' and that Australian real estate re-entered bubble territory 'in 1999 or 2000'. The page does not use the name 'Kavanagh-Putland Index'. Tony O'Brien (late) assisted; his 'Land Monopoly and Income Polarisation in Australia 1950 to 2000' appeared in Progress, September-October 2001, six months before his death. Philip Day (LLB DipTCP PhD, late) was principal author of the LVRG submission to the 1996 National Tax Reform Summit; in 1997/98 the LVRG sponsored a 'National Tax Reform Challenge' prize for the best refutation; Gavin R. Putland was an unsuccessful contestant. Putland was hired by Prosper Australia in 2003 (Communications Officer, later Research Officer); in 2008 he officially assumed the LVRG directorship, merged with the Research Officer role, 'formalising the arrangement that the LVRG is the research arm of Prosper Australia' and making the directorship a paid post for the first time. LVRG describes itself as non-partisan; joint patrons were the late Clyde Cameron AO (Whitlam-era Labor Minister for Labour) and the late Sir Allen Fairhall (Liberal Minister under Menzies and Holt). CURRENT STATUS: 'The Land Values Research Group's work continues today through the Prosper Australia Research Institute'; 'Kavanagh remains active in the LVRG. He blogs at The Depression' (page undated, so currency of this sentence unknown).
